summary: Reports the work of a committee that cleaned up problems in the original Host-Host Protocol, the rules the first ARPANET computers used to set up connections and control data flow. It lists agreed changes to the protocol and discusses at length what a byte means for a connection. It replaced the committee's earlier report in RFC 102.

plainLanguage.summary: The first rules for how computers talk had small bugs, like a game rulebook with unclear rules. A group met, argued about the confusing parts, and wrote down fixes.

questions: what changes were made to the host-host protocol in 1971
what was the host-host protocol glitch cleaning committee
what does rst do in the host-host protocol
subtitle: A 1971 committee's fixes to the first ARPANET Host-Host Protocol, from byte streams to new flow control.

tldr.problem: The original Host-Host Protocol treated a connection as a bare bit stream, which forced expensive bit shifting, and it had flow control and control-message quirks that needed cleaning up.
tldr.mechanism: The committee turned connections into byte streams with a byte size S, changed the message format, added reset commands RST and RRP, replaced the Cease mechanism with separate message and bit allocations, and moved control traffic to link 0.
tldr.outcome: This RFC entirely supersedes RFC 102 and officially modifies Document #1. Later RFCs (111, 124, 132, 154 and 179) updated it in turn.

today: RFC 107 is marked with an unknown status and was updated by RFC 111, RFC 124, RFC 132, RFC 154 and RFC 179. It supersedes RFC 102.

sections.title: The Glitch Cleaning Committee
sections.content:
The Host-Host Protocol Glitch Cleaning Committee met for the second time at UCLA on 8 and 9 March 1971, after canvassing the network community. The first meeting is documented in RFC 102, which this RFC entirely supersedes. The result is an official modification of Document #1, the original protocol specification.

The committee spent the first meeting mostly on the interrupt mechanism and the second almost entirely on the notion of bytes. NCP implementers are told to put the changes in as soon as possible and to report an estimated ready date to Steve Crocker or his secretary.
sections.plainLanguage: A small group of people met twice to fix the confusing parts of the very first network rules, then wrote down what they agreed.

sections.title: Byte Streams and the New Message Format
sections.content:
A connection used to be a bit stream. Now it is a byte stream whose byte size S is carried in the STR command and in every message, with 1 <= S <= 255. The size is constant for the life of the connection, and each message must hold a whole number of bytes.

The message header has fields M1 and M2 (8 bits each, must be zero), S (8 bits, must match the STR) and C, a 16-bit count of bytes in the text. Text starts 72 bits after the start of the message, and a C of zero is legal but meaningless. Message boundaries carry no meaning: a receiver must not expect records or data types to line up with them.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending a stream of single beads, computers now send beads strung in groups of a size they agree on first. The groups of beads in a package do not mean anything special.

sections.title: Reset, Flow Control and the Control Link
sections.content:
Two new one-byte commands, RST (reset) and RRP (reset reply), tell a host to purge all NCP table entries that came from the sender. The receiver answers with RRP, and the sender may then request connections.

The Cease mechanism is dropped and the Imps stop generating the 10HI, 11HI and 12HI messages. Instead, the receiver allocates messages and bits separately. Each side keeps a 16-bit counter for messages and a 32-bit counter for bits, and the sender may not send if either would go below zero. The GVB command now has fields fM and fB, counted in 128ths of the current allocation.

The control link becomes link 0, so old and new protocols can coexist. Control messages use byte size 8, carry at most 120 bytes of text and must hold whole commands. The ECO and ERP commands become 16 bits, and ERR becomes 96 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver now hands out two kinds of tickets, one for how many packages and one for how many beads, and the sender must have both. A reset button lets a computer say forget everything about me and start fresh.

sections.title: Why Bytes? The Committee's Discussion
sections.content:
Bit streams gave maximum generality and minimum efficiency. Receivers had to shift bits to join successive messages, and a sending NCP could not hold text back, because two processes that each answer one bit with one bit could deadlock if a waiting bit were delayed.

The committee settled on an indivisible, fairly small transmission unit, which became the byte. It also noted that a connection can have a sender byte size S and a different receiver byte size R, where R only decides how often the receiving NCP wakes the user process. A receiver may refuse a connection because of its byte size, though the committee strongly suggests NCPs handle all sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: Counting every single bead was slow, so they agreed to move beads in small bundles. The sender and the receiver may each pick their own bundle size.
